edges.description: The childhood lesion (swelling, restricted diffusion) is followed in adults by putaminal atrophy, read by the founding report as a later stage of the same process. This rests on cross-sectional imaging of different individuals, not serial scans.

nodes.description: Childhood-onset, generalized, scarcely progressive chorea is the defining clinical feature. Development and cognition are normal, which initially suggests benign hereditary chorea.

evidence.reference_title: De Novo Mutations in PDE10A Cause Childhood-Onset Chorea with Bilateral Striatal Lesions.
evidence.snippet: Here, we used whole-exome sequencing to unravel the underlying genetic cause in three unrelated individuals with a very similar and unique clinical presentation of childhood-onset chorea and characteristic brain MRI showing symmetrical bilateral striatal lesions.

evidence.reference_title: Familial choreoathetosis due to novel heterozygous mutation in PDE10A.
evidence.snippet: We report a family with multiple affected individuals with childhood onset chorea, striatal abnormalities, and a novel heterozygous mutation, c.1001T>G(p.F334C) in PDE10A which was identified by exome sequencing.

nodes.description: Older individuals show modest putaminal atrophy with normal diffusion, which the founding report interprets as a later stage of the same striatal process that appears as swelling with restricted diffusion in childhood.

evidence.reference_title: De Novo Mutations in PDE10A Cause Childhood-Onset Chorea with Bilateral Striatal Lesions.
evidence.snippet: It is noteworthy that MRI of individual 1 (II-1 in Figure 2A; aged 11 years when scanned) showed slight swelling of the striata (Figure 1A) together with restricted diffusion (Figures 1B and 1C), suggesting an active disease process.

nodes.description: Striatal medium spiny neuron activity depends on cAMP signaling set by adenylyl cyclase 5 synthesis and PDE10A degradation. Without cAMP-stimulated PDE10A activity, cAMP-dependent signaling in MSNs is expected to be poorly braked during dopamine D1 or adenosine A2A receptor stimulation. In cells, PKA substrate phosphorylation after forskolin stimulation was reduced by wild-type PDE10A but not by the GAF-B mutants.

nodes.description: Basal PDE10A hydrolysis of cAMP and cGMP is unchanged, but cAMP binding to GAF-B no longer switches the enzyme into its stimulated ("super-active") state. PDE10A therefore cannot increase cyclic-nucleotide breakdown when cAMP rises, removing a brake on medium spiny neuron activation.

evidence.snippet: 1-NO-cAMP markedly increased (approximately 2.7-fold over the basal levels) the enzyme activity of WT PDE10A, whereas this effect was almost completely lost for both mutant PDE10As (Figure 2E).

nodes.description: A heterozygous missense substitution at Phe300 or Phe334 in the GAF-B regulatory domain of PDE10A, usually arising de novo. The substitution has two separately demonstrated consequences: it disrupts allosteric activation by cAMP, and it causes the enzyme to misfold.

evidence.snippet: Both substitutions affect highly conserved amino acids located in the regulatory GAF-B domain, which, by binding to cAMP, stimulates the activity of the PDE10A catalytic domain.

nodes.description: When overexpressed in HEK293 cells and striatal neurons, the GAF-B mutant forms leave the plasma membrane and accumulate in cytoplasmic, perinuclear aggregates (aggresomes) that recruit p62 and ubiquitin and are cleared by the autophagy-lysosome pathway. Recessive GAF-A variants instead cause mistrafficking and degradation without aggregation, which the authors take as evidence of a distinct mechanism.
